source.filename: 2024-Effect of R-phase on shape recovery speed of Ti-Ni shape memory alloy wire for variable-stiffness mechanism using jamming transition phenomenon.pdf

actuation: Electrical heating (Joule heating / energization at a constant voltage of 0.5 V) for shape memory alloy recovery
Pneumatic evacuation (vacuum / air removal) for jamming transition and air injection for unjamming
constitutive_assumptions: Linear approximation of displacement versus energization time from the start of motion to 50 mm deformation to determine shape recovery velocity
Evaluation of tangential stiffness during shape recovery (EA2) based on the linear slope of the recovery plateau region on tensile stress-strain curves
Engineering stress calculated assuming a constant initial cross-sectional area (force divided by cross-sectional area)
No analytical or numerical continuum constitutive models were developed in the paper
control_variables: Applied heating voltage during shape recovery tests (constant 0.5 V)
Initial bending angle of wire in free-recovery tests (90 degrees)

Specimen gauge lengths (30 mm gauge length with 50 mm total length for tensile tests; 70 mm length with 10 mm clamped end for wire velocity tests; 90 mm gauge length for training and device integration)
Tensile test temperature for shape memory evaluation (363 K, maintained above Af in a thermostatic oil bath)
Tensile strain amplitude during evaluation (5% strain)
Training ambient temperature (353 K, corresponding to Af + 20 K)
Training strain amplitude (3% strain) and number of cycles (50 cycles)
Environmental isolation (glass enclosure around shape recovery test to eliminate wind effects)
Variable-stiffness device composition (outer membrane filled with coarse coffee grounds)
dependent_variables: Shape recovery temperature / reverse transformation finish temperature (Af)
Stress at the start of shape recovery (σA)
Plastic / residual strain after deformation and training cycles (%)
Shape recovery time of the variable-stiffness device (s)
Extent of shape recovery / recovery displacement of the variable-stiffness device (mm)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A variable-stiffness and deformable link combining granular jamming of coffee grounds and a shape memory material can deform to fit objects, stiffen when evacuated, and recover its initial shape upon unjamming and heating.
Ti-Ni shape memory alloy specimens exhibiting R-phase transformation during reverse transformation tend to exhibit higher recovery stress than specimens without R-phase transformation.

Ti-Ni SMA wire specimens exhibiting R-phase transformation display significantly higher shape recovery velocities under electrical heating compared to specimens that do not exhibit R-phase transformation.

High shape recovery velocity in Ti-Ni SMA wires correlates with high stress at the onset of recovery (σA) and low tangential stiffness during recovery (EA2), with EA2 exerting a greater influence on velocity.

A variable-stiffness jamming device utilizing untrained R-phase SMA wire recovers faster than one using non-R-phase wire, but fails to achieve complete recovery (stopping 10 mm short) due to plastic strain accumulation.

Superelastic cyclic training (50 loading-unloading cycles at 3% strain and 353 K) decreases plastic strain from 0.37% to 0.03% without reducing shape recovery velocity, allowing the variable-stiffness device to nearly fully restore its initial shape.

experimental_setup: Heat-treatment setup: Atmospheric furnace heating of 0.9 mm diameter Ti-Ni SMA wires at specified temperatures (723 K or 773 K) and times (0.3 ks, 0.6 ks, 1.2 ks) followed by water quenching, with phase transformation characteristics and Af verified by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).

Electrical heating recovery test: 70 mm straight memorized SMA wire with a 10 mm fixed clamped end, bent 90 degrees, energized at 0.5 V constant voltage inside a glass cage; top-view camera tracked red tape at the wire tip against graph paper, processed using RGB color tracking in LabVIEW.

Tensile testing setup: Shimadzu Autograph AGS-J 5 kN machine equipped with a thermostatic oil bath to maintain ambient temperature (363 K for property evaluation; 353 K for training), load cell for force, and laser displacement meter for displacement.
SMA mechanical training setup: Tensile machine performing 50 repeated loading-unloading cycles at 3% strain amplitude at 353 K on a 90 mm gauge length SMA wire.

Variable-stiffness device setup: A deformable link consisting of coarse coffee grounds enclosed within an outer membrane along with an SMA wire element, operated via internal air evacuation for jamming and air injection plus 0.5 V electrical heating for shape recovery.
future_work: Establishing a clear target recovery velocity for the variable-stiffness device in practical pick-and-place applications
Investigating the influence of different training conditions on the shape-recovery characteristics and performance of Ti-Ni SMA elements to achieve complete shape recovery
independent_variables: Heat-treatment temperature and duration of Ti-Ni SMA wire (untreated, 723 K for 0.6 ks, 723 K for 1.2 ks, and 773 K for 0.3 ks)
Presence versus absence of R-phase transformation during reverse transformation
SMA wire manufacturer / material source (Furukawa Techno Material vs. Nilaco)
Mechanical training status of the SMA wire (untrained vs. cyclically trained for 50 cycles at 3% strain and 353 K)
limitations_inferred: Experiments only evaluated single 0.9 mm diameter wires in a straight geometry; behavior of wire bundles, springs, or complex geometries was not tested.
All recovery velocity measurements were performed under unloaded conditions; performance under external resistive payloads or grasping forces was not evaluated.
Joule heating was conducted at a fixed voltage without active temperature feedback or closed-loop control.
Cooling duration (reset time back to the soft state) was not characterized, which represents a key factor in overall cycle time.
Fatigue endurance and functional degradation beyond 50 training cycles were not evaluated.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The variable-stiffness device incorporating untrained R-phase SMA wire could not achieve full shape recovery, stopping 10 mm short of its initial shape due to plastic strain introduced during deformation.
Even after cyclic training of the SMA wire, the variable-stiffness device did not completely recover its initial shape.
A specific target operating recovery velocity for the variable-stiffness device has not been clearly established.
Untrained Ti-Ni SMA elements exhibited low repeatability due to increasing plastic strain during deformation.
main_results: SMA specimens exhibiting R-phase transformation showed distinctly higher recovery velocities (~2.4 to 2.5 mm/s) than specimens without R-phase (~0.6 to 1.3 mm/s).

Tensile testing demonstrated that high recovery velocity is driven by a combination of high initial recovery stress (σA) and low tangential stiffness during recovery (EA2), with EA2 exerting the dominant influence.

The variable-stiffness device fabricated with R-phase SMA wire (773 K for 0.3 ks) significantly shortened recovery time compared to a device using Nilaco SMA, but suffered from incomplete recovery due to residual plastic strain.
Mechanical training reduced plastic strain from 0.37% to 0.03% (less than one-tenth) without compromising recovery stress or recovery velocity.
The variable-stiffness device using the trained R-phase SMA wire achieved near-complete shape recovery while preserving the high recovery speed.
modeling_methods: Empirical linear regression / approximation of the displacement-time curve up to 50 mm deformation to compute the recovery velocity (slope)
Direct calculation of stress by dividing measured tensile force by wire cross-sectional area
Extraction of tangential stiffness (EA2) as the linear slope of the recovery plateau region from tensile stress-strain curves
performance_metrics: Displacement (mm) as a function of energization time (s)
Stress at the start of shape recovery σA (MPa)
Tangential stiffness during shape recovery EA2 (MPa)
Plastic strain / residual strain (%) after deformation and training cycles
Device recovery time required to reach 10 mm short of initial shape (s)
Shape recovery extent / height achieved by the variable-stiffness device (mm)
possible_gap_implications: Demonstrating that R-phase transformation and training reduce recovery time in SMA-jamming links suggests that faster actuation cycles are feasible, but the absence of loaded dynamic tests means operational speed under payload remains unproven.
Passive cooling of SMA elements enclosed within granular media could offset speed gains obtained during electrical heating recovery, highlighting a gap in thermal dissipation management.
The remaining residual strain even after 50 training cycles indicates that long-term cyclic stabilization under repetitive jamming-unjamming cycles requires further investigation.
paper.research_objective: To investigate the effect of R-phase transformation on the shape recovery velocity of Ti-Ni shape memory alloy wire elements, clarify the underlying mechanical factors (initial recovery stress and tangential stiffness), and improve the operating speed and shape recovery capability of a variable-stiffness device using granular jamming.
paper.research_problem: Variable-stiffness and deformable mechanisms combining shape memory materials and granular jamming operate slowly due to the slow shape recovery velocity of the shape memory alloy (Ti-Ni SMA) element.
paper.robot_type: variable-stiffness and deformable link (variable-stiffness mechanism for attachment to a robot arm for pick-and-place motion)
stiffness_mechanism: Jamming transition phenomenon (granular jamming using coarse coffee grounds)
Shape memory effect / phase transformation of Ti-Ni shape memory alloy (SMA) wire
paper.title: Effect of R-phase on shape recovery speed of Ti-Ni shape memory alloy wire for variable-stiffness mechanism using jamming transition phenomenon
